name: Congress Poland
info: A semi-autonomous Kingdom of Poland created by the Congress of Vienna in 1815 in personal union with the Russian Empire, stripped of its autonomy after the uprisings of 1830 and 1863.

facts.founder: The Congress of Vienna, with Tsar Alexander I as King of Poland; Adam Jerzy Czartoryski worked for its creation
facts.successor: Government General of Warsaw, then the Kingdom of Poland of 1916 under the Central Powers

t: The Kingdom of Poland of 1815 had one of the most liberal constitutions of 19th-century Europe, but the Russian emperors as its kings disregarded the limits on their power.
After the November Uprising of 1830–1831 and the January Uprising of 1863 its autonomy was dismantled and the land was ruled directly as part of the Russian Empire, officially called Vistula Land.
Congress Poland became the most industrialized region of the Russian Empire, with the textile centre of Łódź and Warsaw the empire's third-largest city.
dyk: In January 1831 the Sejm deposed Nicholas I as King of Poland, answering his repeated curtailing of its constitutional rights; he sent Russian troops into the country.
ev: The Congress of Vienna creates the Kingdom of Poland from most of the Duchy of Warsaw, ruled by Tsar Alexander I
Alexander I abolishes freedom of the press and introduces preventive censorship
The Sejm deposes Nicholas I, and the November Uprising is defeated after an 11-month campaign
The Organic Statute repeals the constitution and abolishes the army and the Sejm
The January Uprising breaks out and is crushed within two years
The Russian administration enfranchises the peasants, giving them ownership of their land
A reform divides the land into 10 governorates, and the name Vistula Land comes into official use
The Russian army retreats and the Central Powers occupy the kingdom

sections.foundation:
Between 1772 and 1795 Prussia, the Austrian Empire and the Russian Empire divided the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth in three Partitions of Poland. In 1807 Napoleon created the Duchy of Warsaw as a French client state from land taken from Prussia, and enlarged it at Austria's expense after the Battle of Wagram in 1809. After his defeat in Russia in 1812, Prussia insisted that the duchy be eliminated, while Tsar Alexander I wished to annex it; Austria and the United Kingdom, through Lord Castlereagh, strongly opposed him.

In 1815 the Congress of Vienna took the Duchy of Warsaw from France, gave part of it to Prussia as the Grand Duchy of Posen and made the rest, with Warsaw, a nominally independent Kingdom of Poland ruled by the Russian tsar. Historians call it Congress Poland after the congress. It owed much to Adam Jerzy Czartoryski, who sought to revive the Polish state in alliance with Russia. With 128,500 km2 and about 3.3 million people at first, it was one of the smallest Polish states ever, smaller than the Duchy of Warsaw. Its population was mostly Poles, Polish Jews, ethnic Germans, Ukrainians and Lithuanians, with a small Russian minority, and mainly Roman Catholic.
sections.socioeconomy:
Agriculture made up 70% of the national income, and most farms, the folwarks, were large noble estates worked by landless peasants; exports of wheat and rye stabilized the finances, and Great Britain was an important buyer. From 1822 Prince Francis Xavier Drucki-Lubecki opened the Polish market to the world, built the Augustów Canal between the Narew and Neman to bypass Danzig and Prussian tariffs, and founded the Bank Polski. The first Polish steam mill was built in Warsaw-Solec in 1828 and the first textile machine installed in 1829.

The government drew foreign specialists, mostly Germans, relieved of taxes, and Łódź and towns such as Ozorków and Zduńska Wola grew into one of Europe's largest textile centres, multicultural cities where Germans and Jews were the majority. Congress Poland became the most industrialized region of the Russian Empire and Europe's largest supplier of zinc. After the customs border was abolished in 1851, Warsaw, with its railways and bridges, gained priority in the Russian market and became the empire's third-largest city. The population reached 6.1 million by 1870 and 9,402,253 in the census of 1897.
sections.military:
Under the constitution of 1815 the kingdom had an independent army of its own. Discontent at the rule of Nicholas I broke into the November Uprising: when the Sejm deposed him as King of Poland in January 1831, he sent Russian troops in, and the insurrection was defeated after an 11-month military campaign. The Polish Army was then disbanded, and Poles faced confiscation of property, deportation, forced military service and the closing of their universities. The governor Field Marshal Ivan Paskevich directly controlled the Administrative Council.

In 1863 the January Uprising broke out, and Russia and Prussia signed the Alvensleben Convention on 8 February; the rising lasted two years before it was crushed. Later the governor-general of Warsaw, who commanded the Warsaw Military District, controlled all military forces in the region and could impose death sentences without trial. In the First World War the Russian army first won victories against Austria-Hungary, but after the Gorlice–Tarnów offensive its Great Retreat of 1915 looted and abandoned the kingdom, and it deported hundreds of thousands of inhabitants suspected of collaborating with the enemy.
sections.governance:
The Constitution of the Kingdom of Poland of 1815 made the emperor of Russia king, with a viceroy (namiestnik), a Council of State, an Administrative Council of five ministers and a Sejm that could vote laws. The kingdom had its own currency, budget, penal code and a customs border with Russia, and was one of the few constitutional monarchies of its day. In practice the kings held absolute power and the title of Autocrat. Alexander I gave the viceroy, Grand Duke Konstantin Pavlovich, almost dictatorial powers, abolished press freedom in 1819, ordered Freemasonry abolished in 1821, and from 1825 the Sejm met in secret, while Nikolay Novosiltsev's secret police pursued Polish societies.

Nicholas I, crowned in Warsaw on 24 May 1829, pursued Official Nationality: Orthodoxy, Autocracy and Nationality. After 1831 the Organic Statute of 1832 repealed the constitution; voivodeships became governorates in 1837, the ruble became legal tender in 1841 and the Russian penal code replaced the Polish one. After 1863 Russian became co-official, and in the 1880s Polish was banned from official use and schools. The last namiestnik, Friedrich Wilhelm Rembert von Berg, died in 1874, and the governor-general of Warsaw took his role.
sections.impact:
Congress Poland held most of the ethnic Poles of the Russian Empire, and its history shows the wider fate of the partitioned Polish lands, alongside the Austrian Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria and the Prussian Grand Duchy of Posen. Its liberal constitution, its Sejm and the nobility's tradition of Golden Liberty made the absolute rule Russia wanted hard to establish, and its two great uprisings, in 1830 and 1863, were answered with ever closer integration into Russia.

Russification bore on religion as well as language: the Catholic Church was persecuted, most monasteries were closed and nationalized, papal bulls could not be read without the government's consent, and in 1875 the Uniate Eparchy of Chełm-Belz was united with the Russian Orthodox Church. The land reform of 1864, which gave the peasants ownership, was meant to win the peasantry's loyalty and break the economic power of the rebellious gentry. The kingdom's industry made Warsaw and Łódź major cities, and its territory corresponds roughly to the Lublin, Łódź, Masovian, Podlaskie and Holy Cross Voivodeships of Poland and parts of Lithuania and Belarus.
sections.decline:
The kingdom lost its autonomy in stages. After 1831 it kept the złoty and some privileges of the Administrative Council for a time, but its separate status was gradually eroded; the customs border went in 1851. The January Uprising removed what separate status remained, and the land was incorporated directly into the Russian Empire. From 1867 official Russian usage called it Vistula Land (Privislinskiy kray), to remove Polish national identity from the map, although it was still formally the Kingdom of Poland and the tsars kept the title Tsar of Poland. In 1912 the new Chełm Governorate was split off and attached to the Southwestern Krai to speed its russification.

Russian rule effectively ended with the Great Retreat of 1915, when the Central Powers occupied the region. The Germans set up the Government General of Warsaw, and in 1916 it was succeeded by a short-lived Kingdom of Poland, a client state of the Central Powers with a Regency Council instead of a king. In the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk of March 1918, Russia, by then in civil war, ceded all the Polish lands it had held to the German Empire and Austria-Hungary.

summary: Congress Poland was the Kingdom of Poland set up by the Congress of Vienna in 1815 under the Russian tsar, with a liberal constitution that its kings ignored. After the uprisings of 1830 and 1863 it was absorbed into Russia as Vistula Land, even as it became the empire's most industrialized region, until Russian rule ended in 1915.
references: Davies, Norman, God's Playground: A History of Poland, Vol. 2: 1795 to the Present (Oxford University Press, 1982)
Leslie, R. F., Polish politics and the Revolution of November 1830 (Greenwood Press, 1956)
Zamoyski, Adam, Poland: a history (Hippocrene Books, 2012)

pointDescs.1815: The Congress of Vienna creates the kingdom with a liberal constitution, its own army, currency and Sejm.
pointDescs.1819: Alexander I abolishes freedom of the press and introduces preventive censorship.
pointDescs.1825: Sessions of the Sejm begin to be held in secret as resistance to Russian control grows.
pointDescs.1831: The Sejm deposes Nicholas I; the November Uprising is defeated after an 11-month campaign.
pointDescs.1832: The Organic Statute repeals the constitution and abolishes the army and the Sejm.
pointDescs.1837: The voivodeships are turned into governorates of the Russian administrative system.
pointDescs.1851: The customs border with Russia is abolished, though industry and Warsaw grow.
pointDescs.1863: The January Uprising breaks out and is crushed within two years.
pointDescs.1867: A reform makes ten governorates and the name Vistula Land comes into official use.
pointDescs.1880: In the 1880s Russian becomes the official language and Polish is banned from official use and schools.
pointDescs.1912: The Chełm Governorate is split off and attached to the Southwestern Krai.
pointDescs.1915: The Russian Great Retreat ends Russian rule and the Central Powers occupy the land.

notes: The article dates the end of the namestnik office 1874 or 1875, and the name Vistula Land to 1867, 1883 or 1888: kept as 'from 1867 official usage'.
